source_text: cum Manichaeis dicunt, inesse carni suae mali necessitatem O quam digne Ieremias cum prophetarum choro et sanctorum omnium exclamaret: Quis dabit capiti meo aquam, et oculis meis fontem lacrimarum? gloriosa certamina
pass_a_gloss: When/with Manichaeis they-say, inesse carni his-own of-evil necessity o than/which digne Ieremias when/with prophetarum choro and sanctorum of-all exclamaret: who dabit capiti meo aquam, and oculis meis fontem lacrimarum? gloriosa certamina.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: How fittingly Jeremiah, with the chorus of prophets and all the saints, would cry out: ‘Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?’ (Jeremiah 9:1).
The wickedness of a declining age.
They say with the Manichaeans that a necessity of evil exists in their flesh.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian contrasts opportunity/help with imposed necessity; load-bearing against natural compulsion to sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

bible_refs.note: Linked from Julian's wording or a clear allusion in the excerpt.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
